$comment: The register fetch.py reads. A source with no entry here cannot be fetched, and a source whose bytes do not match its recorded sha256 fails --verify. 'licence_doc' must name a file in this directory; fetch.py checks that it exists before it opens a socket, because a licence written after the download is a licence written to fit.

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:50m rivers and lake centrelines
sources.selection: scalerank <= 5 only. Natural Earth ships several thousand watercourses and this atlas wants the Loire, the Seine, the Rhone, the Garonne and the Danube — the rivers a reader recognises as the shape of a country. Hundreds of tiny streams would be the OpenStreetMap default look, which is the thing this cartography exists not to be.
scalerank <= 4. Geneva, Constance, Balaton, Vanern, Ladoga — the lakes that are part of a country's shape.

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:50m marine polygons (sea and ocean names)
sources.selection: Named seas and oceans only, for the widely tracked uppercase water labels an atlas plate carries. ATLANTIC OCEAN and AEGEAN SEA are geography; drawing them from a list somebody typed would be authoring geography.

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:50m physical geography regions (ranges, plains)
sources.selection: Named ranges and basins — ALPS, PYRENEES, MASSIF CENTRAL — for the italic serif feature labels. This is the layer that lets a reader see where the Alps are before the DEM exists.

sources.dataset: Natural Earth 1:10m named elevation points (summits and depressions)
sources.selection: Named summits inside the extent, 105 of them, and only the highest few in any one frame. THE 1:50m FILE HAS THREE IN ALL OF EUROPE — Elbrus, Mont Blanc and one depression — which is not a layer. A peak with a measured height is the closest this atlas comes to relief without an elevation model, and it is a measurement somebody else made rather than a surface we fitted.

sources.dataset: AWS Terrain Tiles, terrarium encoding, zoom 7 tile 65/45
sources.selection: Zoom 7 and no deeper, and only the six tiles that cover the Chamonix frame. ZOOM IS THE LICENCE HERE: at zoom 9 Tilezen fills Europe with EU-DEM, whose Copernicus attribution this repository has not accepted, and at zoom 10 with four national CC BY datasets. At zoom 7 the land is SRTM and GMTED and the sea is ETOPO1 — three US Government public-domain sets, verified per tile against the service's own x-amz-meta-x-imagery-sources header, which is recorded in `provenance` below. 865 m per pixel at 45 degrees north, which is the resolution a restrained tonal field wants and a long way short of anything that could be mistaken for a GIS hillshade.

blocked.dataset: AWS Terrain Tiles at zoom 9 or deeper (EU-DEM and the national CC BY sets)
blocked.licence: mixed; EU-DEM requires Copernicus attribution, and Austria, Norway and the UK add CC BY / OGL obligations
blocked.reason: The same host and the same URL shape as the permitted zoom-7 tiles, and a different licence. Tilezen switches Europe to EU-DEM at zoom 9 and to the national datasets at zoom 10, so 'one zoom deeper for a bit more detail' is a licence decision wearing the clothes of a quality tweak. The guard is on the URL because that is where the zoom is.

$comment_awaiting: AWAITING_FETCH: rows that are registered, licence-checked and NOT in the repository. The build must run on a host with no internet, so raw bytes are committed — and this environment's proxy refuses every general host, so acquisition is a human step. These are the layers the renderer declares and cannot draw. Each carries the same public-domain terms as the land already here, from the same publisher, so no new licence DECISION is waiting on anybody: only the command. `scripts/map/fetch.py --awaiting` fetches them; `checks.py` asserts each has a licence record and that its file is genuinely absent, so a half-fetched row cannot sit here looking settled.
